summary: The note compares urban green space design strategies in New York, Tokyo, Copenhagen, Singapore, London and Melbourne, showing how green spaces have shifted from luxuries to necessities. It highlights city-specific programs such as Adopt-a-Park, Green Curtains, Green Cycle Routes and Green Corners. It also covers cross-cutting themes of technology, inclusivity, environmental education and citizen participation.
one_line: Comparative overview of how six global cities design, manage and diversify urban green spaces through community, technology, inclusivity and indigenous knowledge.
key_facts: A World Health Organization report dated September 5, 2023 labeled urban green spaces "critical urban infrastructure," similar in importance to roads and utilities.
New York City introduced the "Adopt-a-Park" program on October 15, 2023, giving local communities stewardship over nearby green spaces.
Landscape architect Julia Hernandez said locals who invest in a park are more likely to use and care for it, creating "a virtuous cycle of engagement and upkeep."

Since September 2023, the Tokyo Metropolitan Government has promoted its "Green Curtains" project, encouraging residents and office buildings to grow ivy and other climbing plants on outer walls to cool buildings and improve air quality.
Tokyo emphasizes pocket parks and vertical gardens because space is at a premium, and uses augmented reality apps to guide visitors through pocket parks.
Copenhagen's Green Cycle Routes form a network connecting the city through vegetation-lined green corridors for cyclists and pedestrians.
Urban planner Anders Kærgaard said on September 11, 2023 that integrating transportation with green spaces encourages physical activity and lets urbanites reconnect with nature.
Singapore has embraced the title "Garden City" since the 1960s, with Gardens by the Bay, rooftop gardens and strict greenery replacement rules for developers.
London has eight Royal Parks and is creating 'wild meadows' within them to encourage biodiversity.
On December 1, 2023, London announced the "Green Corners" project to turn neglected urban corners into mini-green spaces, all of which will be accessible.
Melbourne's planners have worked with Aboriginal leaders since late 2023 to integrate traditional land management and prefer low-water indigenous plant species.
New York's "Smart Park" technology embeds sensors in park infrastructure to monitor foot traffic and park health.
Singapore's park areas include inclusive playgrounds for children with different abilities, plus educational signage and biodiversity workshops.
